sources.title: Dash Academy curriculum, subsequent build sequence

claims.text: Dash Platform is a decentralized data-storage and application layer on top of Dash. Developers submit structured state changes governed by schemas rather than arbitrary user-written programs.
Application data lives in Drive as Platform state, hosted by the Platform network rather than in the application's private database or the Core payment ledger.
Platform state can be understood as one large database containing a separate application state for each registered data contract.
A data contract defines an application's stored data schema. A request to store or change data succeeds only when the resulting data matches that schema.

Application records are documents associated with a data contract. Documents contain application fields plus base fields including an identifier, type, revision, contract identifier, and owning identity.
Platform identities contain public keys that prove ownership of data, and state transitions must be signed to prove that an authorized party submitted them.
For document replacement and deletion, Platform checks the existing document's ownership; the Platform tutorial explicitly states that only the document owner can delete it.

The owning identity controls ordinary edits to a mutable document, but the data contract may make a document type immutable or non-deletable. Creation permission is separate and may allow anyone, only the contract owner, or nobody.
The identity that registers a data contract owns it, and only that identity may submit compatible updates to the contract schema.
Dash Core is the layer-1 payment system, while Dash Platform supplies structured application storage, identities, names, and document operations.

A feature that only sends or receives Dash belongs to Core. A feature that must store shared, queryable records and let identities authorize changes belongs on Platform. A request requiring arbitrary user-written on-chain execution is not met by Platform's documented schema-and-state-transition model.
DPNS is an application built on Platform that registers human-readable names and associates them with identities, providing a concrete capability that Dash Core alone does not supply.
Dashnote is an official example of a Platform application: users create, edit, and delete their own notes while other identities' notes can be browsed read-only.

The later curriculum follows Platform's dependency order: connect to the network, create and fund an identity, register a name, define and register a data contract, operate documents, and then work with tokens.

uncertainties.topic: How far this module should extend into the broader build-fit comparison assigned to module 4
uncertainties.resolution: The lesson uses a narrow routing rule based on Core payments versus Platform application state and leaves product categories, economics, privacy, and governance to module 4.

uncertainties.topic: Whether authorization can be summarized as only the owner being allowed to change a document
uncertainties.resolution: The lesson says signed identity authorization and contract rules both apply, with the current owner controlling ordinary replace and delete operations.

uncertainties.topic: How specifically to describe what the learner will build
uncertainties.resolution: The lesson describes the curriculum sequence without inventing a named final product; DPNS and Dashnote appear only as existing examples.
